title_candidates: They Hunted the Last Stormglass Dragon Child… Until the Disgraced Keeper Chose to Protect It
The Last Stormglass Child Trusts the Keeper Everyone Else Calls a Traitor
A Hunted Dragon Child. A Disgraced Keeper. One Storm That Can Save Them Both.
logline: A disgraced royal beastkeeper rescues the last stormglass dragon child from the navy that made her a scapegoat, then must return to the kingdom that condemned her before the child is weaponized and the sea storm destroys both their homes.
audience_promise: A cinematic creature-protection fantasy: visible vulnerable dragon child, costly protective love, injustice and public reversal, storm-scale spectacle, and a warm found-family/belonging payoff.

emotional_engine.wound: Mira was publicly branded a traitor after a nursery fire she did not start, losing her home, rank, and every creature she loved.
emotional_engine.want: Mira wants to survive far from the kingdom and never bond with another creature she can lose.
emotional_engine.need: She needs to accept protection as love rather than weakness and risk attachment again.
emotional_engine.injustice: The admiral who caused the nursery fire now hunts the last dragon child and plans to use it as a navigation weapon.
emotional_engine.protective_counterforce: Mira repeatedly chooses the dragon child's safety over her own exile, freedom, and revenge.
emotional_engine.belonging_payoff: Mira, the child, and the coastal villagers form a protected home where the child is no longer property and Mira is publicly restored.
emotional_engine.secret_or_power_asymmetry: Mira knows the child's stormcall can calm the sea only when it feels safe; the navy thinks pain can control it.
emotional_engine.cost_of_failure: The child becomes a weapon, the storm wall collapses, and both the capital and fishing coast are flooded.

protagonist.identity: Mira Vale, ex-royal beastkeeper living as a lighthouse laborer
protagonist.vulnerability: Social disgrace, fear of attachment, and a burn scar that the navy uses to identify her
protagonist.capability: Reads creature fear, weather behavior, and body language better than anyone in the kingdom
protagonist.agency_first_action: She cuts the dragon child free from a weighted capture net even though helping it exposes her identity
protagonist.transformation: From self-protective exile to public protector willing to trust and be trusted again

opening_event.first_10_seconds: A weighted navy net crashes into black water; inside it, a palm-sized translucent blue dragon child claws at the ropes and cries silently.
opening_event.first_60_seconds: Mira recognizes the creature's panic, sees the royal brand on the net, and cuts it free while soldiers close in on the shore.
opening_event.first_5_minutes: The child bonds to Mira after she shields it from crossbow fire; its fear calls the first impossible storm wall, proving the title promise visually.
opening_event.dramatic_question: Can Mira keep the child emotionally and physically safe long enough to expose the admiral before fear turns the storm against everyone?

theme_lane.mythic_creature: stormglass dragon child whose emotional state shapes sea weather
theme_lane.family_or_heir_hook: last surviving creature child and deposed protector becoming chosen family

nearest_failures: Epic Earthquake: diffuse spectacle before relational anchor
The Next Show ARKAN: abstract quest lore before embodied stakes
Nov underperformers: lore/court exposition before wound-care loop
mitigations: Open on the child in visible peril, not mythology.
Make every spectacle scene threaten or protect the child/Mira relationship.
Limit exposition to facts that change immediate protection choices.
Each act gives Mira an active protective decision and a cost.
End with belonging and public restoration, not only punishment.
counterexamples_checked: Epic One Last Phone Call proves a strong opening alone cannot overcome channel-contract mismatch; therefore creature/protector fit is explicit.
The Next Show Sinbad proves serialization/continuation can work after a major setpiece payoff; this film still resolves its core emotional arc.

packaging.thumbnail_single_read: Close protective hands around a glowing translucent dragon child while a storm-lit naval fleet approaches behind them.
packaging.curiosity_gap: Why is the kingdom hunting a creature child, and why is the accused traitor the only one it trusts?
packaging.visual_before_after: cold netted creature in darkness vs warm glowing child protected in hands
packaging.title_thumbnail_mismatch_risk: Low if the dragon child and protection relationship are visually dominant; avoid making the navy/army the main read.

evidence_boundaries: Observational evidence informs the design but does not prove CTR or retention causality.
The concept is original; it uses mechanisms rather than copying plot, dialogue, characters, or thumbnail artwork.
No AI-generated media has been produced yet; production feasibility still requires provider validation.

meaning_carrier.object_or_space: weighted capture net, stormglass scales, and the beastkeeper lullaby
meaning_carrier.closing_reversal: the net logic is broken by sanctuary, stormglass becomes a free arch rather than a weapon, and the lullaby is completed by free creature voices
meaning_carrier.final_sequence_use: the final storm vault inversion and sunlit stormglass arch prove that safety, not force, controls the sea
